title: Chapter 23 — The Lee Shore
paragraphs: Some chapters back, a man named Bulkington was mentioned — a tall, recently landed sailor encountered at the inn in New Bedford.

When, on that shivering winter's night, the Pequod thrust her vengeful bows into the cold, malicious waves, who should I see standing at her helm but Bulkington! I looked at the man with sympathetic awe and dread. Here was someone who, in midwinter, having just landed from a dangerous four-year voyage, could so restlessly push off again for yet another stormy term at sea. The land seemed to scorch his feet. The most wondrous things are always the ones that cannot be spoken; deep memories yield no epitaphs; this six-inch chapter is the stoneless grave of Bulkington. Let me say only that it went with him as with the storm-tossed ship that drives miserably along a lee shore. The port would gladly give shelter; the port is compassionate; in the port there is safety, comfort, a hearth, supper, warm blankets, friends — everything that is kind to our mortal selves. But in that gale, the port, the land, is that ship's direst danger. She must flee all hospitality. One touch of land, even if it only grazed the keel, would make her shudder through and through. With all her might she crowds on every sail to get offshore, and in doing so fights the very winds that would gladly blow her homeward. She seeks the lashed sea's landlessness again, rushing forlornly into danger for the sake of refuge — her only friend her bitterest enemy!

Do you understand now, Bulkington? Do you seem to catch glimpses of that mortally unbearable truth — that all deep, earnest thinking is nothing but the brave effort of the soul to keep the open independence of her sea, while the wildest winds of heaven and earth conspire to cast her on the treacherous, enslaving shore?

But since the highest truth lives only in landlessness — shoreless and boundless as God — it is better to perish in that howling infinity than to be ingloriously dashed against the lee shore, even if that shore meant safety! For who, worm-like, would crawl like a coward to land! Terrors of the terrible! Is all this agony in vain? Take heart, take heart, O Bulkington! Bear up grimly, demigod! Up from the spray of your ocean death — straight up — leaps your apotheosis!
